lines.text: In a mixture of experts, a router decides which experts handle a token.
It is a small network, trained to send tokens to the experts that handle them best.
Which is the whole problem. If every token goes to the best-fitting expert, one expert wins.
It gets all the training signal. The others get nothing, and they go stale.
So the router is given a second objective: send a balanced share of tokens everywhere.
That is the load-balancing loss, added to the training loss.
It is a hack in the truest sense. The router is told to do something other than the thing it was built for.
And the tension is real. Fit the tokens perfectly and the experts go stale. Balance them perfectly and the routing goes bad.
So every router sits somewhere on that trade-off.
Push too hard and the router starts sending tokens to worse experts, to satisfy the balance.
Push too little and you are back to one popular expert doing all the work.
The coefficient on that loss is the knob. One number trades quality against capacity.
The router is trained to be good at routing, and punished for being good at it.
